body.p: Applicant replies to the non-final Office Action dated July 29, 2021, in which this Reply is filed within three months. Claims 1-20 stand rejected. Independent claims 1 and 11 are currently amended. Claim 13 is canceled without prejudice or disclaimer. Claim 21 is new. Support for the present amendments and the new claim can be found in the originally filed specification, claims, and drawings. Reconsideration is respectfully requested. Reconsideration is respectfully requested.
Rejections under Q 102

Claims 1-9, 11-12, and 15-16 are rejected under 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by U.S. Patent No. 4,887,016 ("Malick"). Applicant respectfully disagrees with the rejections but amends certain claims solely to expedite prosecution.
Claim ]
The Office Action asserts on page 2 that Malick discloses "a first cargo handling robot

(10)" and "a second cargo handling robot (10A), wherein the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot are configured to transport a cargo unit (47 and 72) from a first position to a second position."

First, it is unclear why the Office Action asserts that the claimed "cargo unit" is disclosed by both Malick's "sensor assembly 47" and "boxes 72." It appears the Office Action impermissibly interprets Applicant's claimed "cargo unit" as two separate and independent devices of Malick. For example, claim 1 provides the first and second cargo handling robots are configured to transport the same cargo unit (i.e., "a cargo unit"), whereas it appears the rejection merely asserts that Malick's robots 10 and 10A are configured to separately transport "sensor assembly 47" and "boxes 72."

Second, Applicant submits that Malick fails to teach both Malick's "robot 10" and Malick's "robot 10A" are configured to transport the same cargo unit. Rather, Malick teaches two different robot designs (i.e., 10 and 10A) where one or the other is used depending on the circumstances of the manufacturing facility. More particularly, Malick recites in col. 4, 11. 10-24, "FIG. 2 illustrates a second embodiment of the present invention in which the robot 10A is mounted upon a motorized wheeled vehicle 21. Because the motorized wheeled vehicle 21 is much more expensive than the pallet 16 and because most manufacturing facilities have a fork lift readily available, the additional expense required to purchase a forklift is rarely required; therefore, the embodiment illustrated in FIG. 1 is the preferred embodiment for most

applications. However, in applications in which the robot must be operated in a hostile environment whereat use of a man-operated fork lift is not feasible, such as, for example, when the robot is operated in an area of high radioactivity, use of the motorized wheeled vehicle 22 illustrated in FIG. 2 is necessitated."

Applicant amends Claim 1 herein to recite, "the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot are configured to simultaneously transport a cargo unit from a first position to a second position."

Applicant submits that Malick fails to disclose or contemplate at least "the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot are configured to simultaneously transport a cargo unit from a first position to a second position." For example, Malick merely teaches two different robot designs that operate independently of one another and where one or the other is used depending on the circumstances of the manufacturing facility.

Based upon the foregoing, claim 1 is allowable over Malick. All claims that depend from claim 1 are thereby also allowable over Malick for the above-noted reasons. There is therefore no need to separately address the patentability of each of these claims and/or the Patent Office's interpretation in relation to any of these claims or any of the references of record in relation thereto.
The Office Action asserts on page 3 that "Malick discloses [the limitations of claim 11] as discussed above in the rejection to claims 1-9."

Applicant amends claim 11, similar to claim 1, to recite "the cargo handling robot is configured to communicate with a second cargo handling robot so as to simultaneously move the cargo unit together with the second cargo handling robot."

Applicant submits that Malick fails to disclose or contemplate at least "the cargo handling robot is configured to communicate with a second cargo handling robot so as to simultaneously move the cargo unit together with the second cargo handling robot" as provided in claim 11. For example, as discussed above with respect to claim 1, Malick fails to disclose or contemplate two cargo handling robots configured to simultaneously transport a cargo unit from a first position to a second position. In contrast, Malick merely teaches two different robot designs that operate independently of one another and where one or the other is used depending on the circumstances of the manufacturing facility.

Based upon the foregoing, claim 11 is allowable over Malick. All claims that depend from claim 11 are thereby also allowable over Malick for the above-noted reasons. There is therefore no need to separately address the patentability of each of these claims and/or the Patent Office's interpretation in relation to any of these claims or any of the references of record in relation thereto.
Rejections under Q 103
Claims 17-20 are rejected under 103 as being unpatentable over Malick. Applicant traverses the rejection.

The Office Action has not set forth a prima facie obviousness rejection based on Malick. According to M.P.E.P. §2142, "[t]he examiner bears the initial burden of factually supporting any prima facie conclusion of obviousness." Furthermore, "[t]he Supreme Court in KSRInt'l Co. v. Teleflexlnc., 550 U.S. 538, 418 (2007) noted that the analysis supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 should be made explicit." Id. "[R]ejections on obviousness cannot be sustained with mere conclusory statements; instead, there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness." Id., citing In re Kahn, 441 F.3d 977, 988, (Fed. Cir. 2006); see also KSR, 550 U.S. at 418 (quoting Federal Circuit statement with approval).

For the Examiner to rely upon Malick, he must actually provide some articulated reason why this reference purportedly renders the claims obvious under § 103. The Examiner has not explained what specific feature of the claims Malick allegedly obviates. As a result, Applicant is not in a position to properly respond to the Office Action's statement.

For example, Applicant submits the Office Action has failed to provide sufficient rationale to support a conclusion of obviousness. The entirety of the Office Action's rejection of claims 17-20 can be found in five lines on page 4 which recites "the recited method steps for moving a cargo unit is considered to be obvious to Malick, since Malick discloses all of the structural limitations in the claims as discussed above. It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the invention to have performed the claimed method by moving screws with the robots as disclosed in the apparatus of Malick for the purpose of providing an efficient means of operating assembly lines" (emphasis added).
First, Malick does not teach moving "screws" with robots as asserted by the Office Action. It is unclear what is meant by this portion of the rationale of the 35 U.S.C. rejection.
Second, the Examiner fails to address the specific feature of the claims that Malick allegedly discloses.

For example, claim 17 recites "A method of moving a cargo unit via multiple cargo handling robots." As discussed above with respect to claim 1, Malick fails to disclose or contemplate moving a cargo unit via multiple cargo handling robots. In contrast, a single robot 10 of Malick conveys the boxes 72.

Claim 17 further recites, "transmitting, via a network, a first position to a first cargo handling robot and a second cargo handling robot; moving the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot to the first position; attaching the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot to the cargo unit at the first position; transmitting, via the network, a second position to the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot; and moving, via the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot, the cargo unit to the second position, wherein the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot transport the cargo unit horizontally about a cargo deck in response to moving from the first position to the second position." As discussed above with respect to claim 1, Malick does not disclose or contemplate moving, via multiple robots, a cargo unit from a first position to a second position, nor would it be obvious to do so. In stark contrast, Malick recites in col. 5, 11. 37-40, "boxes 72 are conveyed in a sequential fashion to a work station where the box remains stationary while the robot 10 operates to tighten a plurality of bolts 74 on a flange 75 at one side of the box."
Applicant submits that Malick fails to make obvious each and every aspect of independent claim 17. Thus, Applicant requests that the rejection under § 103 in view of Malick be withdrawn.

Additionally, dependent claims 18-20 depend from independent claim 17, and Applicant thus asserts that dependent claims 18-20 are patentable for at least the same reasons for differentiating independent claim 17, as well as in view of their own respective features. Applicant respectfully requests that this rejection be withdrawn.

In view of the above remarks, Applicant respectfully submits that all pending claims are allowable and requests allowance of the pending claims. The Examiner is invited to telephone the undersigned at the Examiner's convenience, if that would help further prosecution of the subject application. Applicant authorizes and respectfully request that any fees due or overpayments be charged or credited to Deposit Account No. 19-2814. This statement does NOT authorize payment of the issue fee.
Respectfully submitted,
